scenes.narration: Every river on Earth is fresh water. So why is the ocean salty enough to make you sick if you drink it?
scenes.headline: Why salty?

scenes.narration: It starts with rain. Rainwater is slightly acidic, and as it falls on land, it slowly breaks down rock.
scenes.headline: It starts with rain

scenes.narration: That process pulls out tiny amounts of minerals, like sodium and chloride, and rivers carry them all the way to the sea.
scenes.headline: Rivers carry minerals

scenes.narration: Here's the trick. When the sun heats the ocean, only the water evaporates. The salt stays behind.
scenes.headline: Water leaves, salt stays

scenes.narration: Underwater volcanoes and vents on the sea floor add even more dissolved minerals to the mix.
scenes.headline: Help from below

scenes.narration: Repeat that for hundreds of millions of years, and you get an ocean that is about three and a half percent salt.
scenes.headline: 3.5% salt

scenes.narration: So the ocean is basically the Earth's collection jar for minerals. Follow for more everyday science in under a minute.
scenes.headline: Earth's salt jar
